title: Entering the era of lattice SNARKs – with a faster, post-quantum Jolt - a16z crypto
gist: a16z's new Lattice Jolt zkVM swaps elliptic-curve cryptography (Dory) for a lattice-based commitment scheme (Akita), making the same zkVM post-quantum, 2-10x faster, and producing the smallest proofs of any post-quantum zkVM (under 100 KB) — evidence the authors use to argue lattice-based SNARKs, not hash-based ones, will become the dominant post-quantum path, mirroring what already happened with digital signatures.

insights.claim: a16z's Lattice Jolt release swaps the cryptographic foundation of the Jolt zkVM from elliptic curves to lattices, simultaneously making it post-quantum, 2-3x faster for prover and verifier, and producer of the shortest proofs of any post-quantum zkVM (under 100 KB).
insights.speaker: Markos Georghiades, Justin Thaler, Andrew Tretyakov, and Michael Zhu
insights.so_what: A single cryptographic swap delivering security, speed, and size gains simultaneously (rather than trading one for another) signals lattice-based zkVMs may leapfrog hash-based post-quantum alternatives in production use.
insights.quote:
It makes Jolt post-quantum.
It makes the prover and verifier 2x-3x faster.
It gives Jolt the shortest proofs of any post-quantum zkVM: under 100 KB today
insights.locator: Today we are releasing Lattice Jolt

insights.claim: Lattice Jolt's new polynomial commitment scheme, Akita, replaces Jolt's prior scheme Dory and is built on the lattice assumption Module-SIS, targeting a full 128 bits of security.
insights.speaker: Markos Georghiades, Justin Thaler, Andrew Tretyakov, and Michael Zhu
insights.so_what: Investors tracking ZK infrastructure should note Dory (the elliptic-curve dependency) is now obsolete inside Jolt, and Akita is the new load-bearing primitive to watch for adoption elsewhere.
insights.quote: Lattice Jolt replaces Dory with Akita, a new polynomial commitment scheme based on the lattice assumption Module-SIS.

insights.claim: Akita was developed and implemented primarily by researchers and engineers at LayerZero, in collaboration with Carnegie Mellon University, the University of Southern California, and a16z crypto's own teams.
insights.speaker: Markos Georghiades, Justin Thaler, Andrew Tretyakov, and Michael Zhu
insights.so_what: LayerZero's team building core lattice cryptography (beyond its bridging/messaging product) signals the protocol is investing in fundamental cryptographic R&D, a data point for anyone assessing LayerZero's technical depth or partnerships.
insights.quote: Akita’s development and implementation was led by researchers and engineers at LayerZero, in collaboration with researchers at Carnegie Mellon University, the University of Southern California, and our engineering and research teams here at a16z crypto.

insights.claim: The core driver of Lattice Jolt's speedup is that elliptic curves forced Jolt to operate over 256-bit fields while lattice cryptography reaches comparable security over 128-bit fields, and since the prover's work is dominated by multiplying large field elements, halving the field size makes each multiplication several times faster.
insights.speaker: Markos Georghiades, Justin Thaler, Andrew Tretyakov, and Michael Zhu
insights.so_what: This is a generalizable mechanism: any SNARK/zkVM system bottlenecked on elliptic-curve field arithmetic could see similar multi-x speedups by migrating to lattice-based 128-bit fields.
insights.quote: Elliptic curves forced Jolt to work over 256-bit fields; lattice cryptography achieves comparable security over 128-bit fields.

insights.claim: On the same laptop, curve-based Jolt improved from about 700,000 to over 1 million RISC-V cycles per second through prior optimizations, while Lattice Jolt (CPU-only) now proves over 2 million cycles per second, and with an Apple Metal GPU implementation, Lattice Jolt reaches over 10 million cycles per second on a MacBook (versus curve-based Jolt on Metal at about 4 million).
insights.speaker: Markos Georghiades, Justin Thaler, Andrew Tretyakov, and Michael Zhu
insights.so_what: A roughly 10x throughput jump in one release (1M to 10M cycles/sec on consumer hardware) is a concrete, checkable performance benchmark for anyone evaluating zkVM competitiveness against Jolt.
insights.quote: GPU-accelerated Lattice Jolt proves over 10 million RV64IMAC cycles per second on a MacBook.

insights.claim: Four years ago, proving a computation with a SNARK prover cost millions of times more than simply running it; Lattice Jolt has brought that overhead down to roughly 10,000x, with further protocol and engineering optimizations still available.
insights.speaker: Markos Georghiades, Justin Thaler, Andrew Tretyakov, and Michael Zhu
insights.so_what: The multi-order-of-magnitude reduction in proving overhead over four years is the trend line to extrapolate when modeling when ZK proving becomes cheap enough for mainstream on-chain or mobile use cases.
insights.quote: Lattice Jolt brings that overhead down to roughly 10,000x. And this is still not the end; clear engineering and protocol optimizations remain on the table.
insights.locator: To put those numbers in perspective

insights.claim: Lattice Jolt produces proofs under 100 KB, substantially smaller than other post-quantum zkVMs whose proofs range from over 200 KB to roughly 600 KB or more.
insights.speaker: Markos Georghiades, Justin Thaler, Andrew Tretyakov, and Michael Zhu
insights.so_what: Smaller proofs directly cut on-chain verification and bandwidth costs; a 2-6x proof-size advantage over competing post-quantum zkVMs is a durable moat if verification cost becomes a competitive axis for ZK infra.
insights.quote: At under 100 KB, Lattice Jolt proofs are already substantially smaller than those of other post-quantum zkVMs, whose proofs range from over 200 KB to roughly 600 KB or more.
insights.locator: Proof size matters just as much as prover speed

insights.claim: Switching to lattices dropped Jolt's prover memory usage from about 300 bytes per cycle to 200 bytes per cycle, which the authors say makes it feasible to prove millions of RISC-V cycles directly on a mobile phone.
insights.speaker: Markos Georghiades, Justin Thaler, Andrew Tretyakov, and Michael Zhu
insights.so_what: Mobile-feasible proving at millions of cycles opens client-side ZK use cases (private mobile apps, on-device attestation) that were previously memory-constrained.
insights.quote: The switch to lattices also improves Jolt’s already best-in-class memory usage, dropping the prover’s space usage from about 300 bytes per cycle to 200. This means you can prove millions of RISC-V cycles on a mobile phone.
insights.locator: Proof size matters just as much as prover speed

insights.claim: The authors argue the SNARK ecosystem is repeating a transition digital signatures already went through: hash-based signatures are the conservative choice, but the world has moved primarily to lattice-based signatures because they are shorter and faster — ML-DSA signatures run a few kilobytes versus the NIST hash-based alternative SLH-DSA being several times larger.
insights.speaker: Markos Georghiades, Justin Thaler, Andrew Tretyakov, and Michael Zhu
insights.so_what: Use the signatures market as a leading indicator for where SNARK cryptography is headed: lattice-based primitives winning on size/speed despite being the 'newer' assumption family.
insights.quote:
ML-DSA signatures are on the order of a few kilobytes.
The NIST-standardized hash-based alternative, SLH-DSA, is several times larger.
insights.locator: The case for lattices over hashing

insights.claim: ML-KEM, the primary post-quantum key-establishment standard NIST finalized in 2024, is already deployed by default in major browsers, messaging apps, and a large share of TLS connections on the web, showing lattice-based cryptography has already won the encryption/key-exchange category outright since no hash-based option exists there.
insights.speaker: Markos Georghiades, Justin Thaler, Andrew Tretyakov, and Michael Zhu
insights.so_what: Lattice-based ML-KEM is arguably the most battle-tested post-quantum primitive already in mass production, which the authors use as evidence that lattice-based SNARKs are not a speculative bet but following an already-validated infrastructure migration.
insights.quote: ML-KEM — the primary key-establishment standard NIST finalized in 2024 — is already deployed by default in major browsers, messaging apps, and a large share of TLS connections on the web.

insights.claim: The authors predict that, following the pattern set by digital signatures, lattice-based SNARKs will become the most deployed post-quantum SNARK option, even though the SNARK community's production attention has so far gone almost entirely to hash-based SNARKs.
insights.speaker: Markos Georghiades, Justin Thaler, Andrew Tretyakov, and Michael Zhu
insights.so_what: This is the article's central forward-looking bet: teams building post-quantum ZK infra today around hash-based SNARKs may be optimizing for a category the authors expect to lose share to lattice-based systems like Lattice Jolt.
insights.quote: But if digital signatures are any guide, lattice-based SNARKs will become the most deployed post-quantum option.

insights.claim: Most hash-based SNARK deployments today rely on SNARK-friendly algebraic hash constructions like Poseidon (rather than standard non-algebraic hashes) to make proving hash evaluations cheap, but these algebraic constructions are far more structured than standard hash functions and their cryptanalysis is much less mature, undermining the claim that hash-based SNARKs are the 'conservative' post-quantum choice.
insights.speaker: Markos Georghiades, Justin Thaler, Andrew Tretyakov, and Michael Zhu
insights.so_what: Teams and investors treating hash-based SNARKs as the 'safe' post-quantum default should scrutinize whether the specific hash function used is algebraic (like Poseidon) — the security story is weaker than the label suggests.
insights.quote: In short, we do not have confidence in the security of algebraic hash functions. Despite this, they are used pervasively in production SNARK systems today.
insights.locator: There is also a misconception worth clearing up here

insights.claim: The Ethereum Foundation recently announced it is moving away from algebraic hash functions in its SNARK/proving systems, which the authors cite as a sign of growing industry recognition of the risk these constructions carry.
insights.speaker: Markos Georghiades, Justin Thaler, Andrew Tretyakov, and Michael Zhu
insights.so_what: A concrete, checkable signal: track whether other major protocols follow Ethereum Foundation's move away from algebraic hashes, which would corroborate the lattice-migration thesis.
insights.quote: in a sign of progress, the Ethereum Foundation recently announced that it is moving away from them.
insights.locator: Despite this, they are used pervasively

insights.claim: Hash-based SNARKs structurally cannot reach a full 128 bits of security over a 128-bit field because their soundness error scales like n/|F| (statement size over field size); proving a billion-step statement over a 128-bit field loses about 30 bits of security, dropping under 100 bits, whereas Lattice Jolt's soundness error scales only like log(n)/|F|, preserving nearly the full 128 bits for the same statement size.
insights.speaker: Markos Georghiades, Justin Thaler, Andrew Tretyakov, and Michael Zhu
insights.so_what: Many production hash-based SNARKs marketed at '128-bit security' may actually deliver well under 100 bits at large statement sizes — a concrete technical due-diligence check for anyone evaluating a ZK system's real security level versus its marketing claim.
insights.quote: So over a 128-bit field, proving a billion-step statement loses about 30 bits of security, dropping under 100 bits. Instead, Lattice Jolt’s soundness error scales like log(n)/|F| — keeping nearly the full 128 bits of security over the same field
insights.locator: Even hash-based SNARKs that avoid the above conjectures

insights.claim: The authors state Jolt will not be tied to a single cryptographic foundation and intend to maintain curve-based, lattice-based, and eventually hash-based versions, arguing different assumptions and performance profiles suit different deployment settings.
insights.speaker: Markos Georghiades, Justin Thaler, Andrew Tretyakov, and Michael Zhu
insights.so_what: This signals a15z/Jolt is hedging cryptographic-assumption risk rather than betting the whole zkVM on lattices, which matters for developers choosing Jolt as infrastructure across different threat models.
insights.quote: Our view has always been that Jolt should not be tied to one cryptographic foundation. We should have mature, performant SNARKs based on curves, hashes, and lattices.
insights.locator: One Jolt, three foundations: curves, lattices, and hashes

insights.claim: The planned hash-based version of Jolt is expected to be inferior to the curve- and lattice-based versions — worse space efficiency and bigger proofs — because the most promising hash-based SNARKs work over binary fields, which are convenient for proving hash evaluations but mismatched with how CPUs perform arithmetic, making CPU multiplication proofs expensive.
insights.speaker: Markos Georghiades, Justin Thaler, Andrew Tretyakov, and Michael Zhu
insights.so_what: This is a specific technical reason to expect hash-based zkVMs to lag on general-purpose CPU workloads even as they remain viable for hash-heavy or recursive proving tasks.
insights.quote: But a hash-based version — compared to curve-based and lattice-based Jolt — will have worse space efficiency, bigger proofs, and a variety of complications.
insights.locator: We will build a hash-based version of Jolt

insights.claim: Elliptic-curve-based Jolt already exploited cheap commitments to sparse vectors (vectors that are mostly zero or small), and lattice commitments preserve this same property, which is why Akita could swap in for Dory while leaving the rest of the Jolt architecture intact.
insights.speaker: Markos Georghiades, Justin Thaler, Andrew Tretyakov, and Michael Zhu
insights.so_what: This sparse-vector-commitment compatibility is the structural reason the lattice swap was low-risk architecturally — a reusable design principle for anyone porting other curve-based SNARK systems to post-quantum lattice commitments.
insights.quote: Lattice commitments have the same property: Committing to a vector is cheap when most of its entries are zero or small, and Jolt commits almost exclusively to such vectors.
insights.locator: Jolt is unusually well positioned for this transition

insights.claim: For client-side proving of 'small' statements (the domain currently dominated by hand-optimized circuits), the authors define the key competitive bar as generating a proof on a phone in under about a second, and state Jolt is already on the edge of achieving this with more speedups still in the pipeline.
insights.speaker: Markos Georghiades, Justin Thaler, Andrew Tretyakov, and Michael Zhu
insights.so_what: Sub-second mobile proving would let a general-purpose zkVM like Jolt displace hand-tuned circuits in consumer privacy apps — worth tracking as a concrete milestone for when general-purpose ZK becomes viable at consumer scale.
insights.quote: the key bar to clear is generating proofs on a phone in under a second or so. Jolt is on the edge of achieving this already, with plenty more speedups in the pipeline.
insights.locator: For the “small” statements relevant to client-side proving

source_meta.author: Markos Georghiades, Justin Thaler, Andrew Tretyakov, and Michael Zhu
